item.title: Show GN: 아크릴 – 브라우저와 내 컴퓨터에서 일하는 사무용 AI 에이전트
item.content:encoded:
안녕하세요. 아크릴 공동창업자 권우성입니다. 마이크로소프트에서 엔지니어로 일했던 동료와 함께 만든 사무용 AI 에이전트, 아크릴을 오늘 공개합니다.

  1. 한글, 워드, 엑셀, 파워포인트 파일을 무료로 편집할 수 있어요. 쓰던 파일을 열어 직접 고치다가 “이 표에 이번 달 실적도 넣어 줘” 하고 AI에게 맡길 수 있습니다. AI가 표와 문단, 셀을 구분해서 필요한 곳을 고칠 수 있도록 편집기부터 다시 설계했어요.

  2. 자료가 많을 땐 폴더째 맡기면 돼요. 파일을 하나씩 올릴 필요 없이 내 컴퓨터에서 작업할 폴더를 고르면 됩니다. 예를 들어 견적서가 여러 개 들어 있는 폴더를 열고 “업체마다 납기가 어떻게 다른지 정리해 줘”라고 할 수 있어요. 어떤 폴더를 AI에게 보여 줄지도 직접 정합니다.

item.content:encoded:
• 사용자가 Safari 설정을 바꾸지 않아도 120 FPS로 반응하는 웹 UI를 구현함. 네이티브 스크롤에서 고빈도 입력을 얻고, OffscreenCanvas로 그려 Liquid Glass 탭 바와 드래그 상호작용을 만듦
  • 스크롤은 JavaScript 왕복 없이 별도 스레드의 컴포지터가 처리하므로, 스크롤 영역을 입력 컨트롤러로 활용하면 네이티브 관성, 바운스, 스냅 동작을 가져올 수 있음
  • 입력만 120 Hz로 받아도 일반 DOM 갱신은 60 Hz에 묶임. OffscreenCanvas가 다음 페이지 렌더링을 기다리지 않고 프레임을 전달하는 WebKit 구현을 활용해 출력 제한도 우회함

item.title: Show GN: gpgpru - 고2가 만들어본 gpgpu crate
item.content:encoded:
제 노트북은 Intel Iris Xe, 내장 그래픽 카드밖에 없어 성능이 넉넉지 않지만, 혼자서 로컬 모델이나 AI 연산, 아니면 간단한 GPGPU 코딩을 해보고 싶을 때가 많았습니다. 매번 시도해보려할 때마다 100시간 이상의 튜토리얼 영상을 보면서 경악하곤 했었죠... 물론 CUDA가 표준이지만, 저는 어떻게든 범용적인 GPGPU programming을 간단하게 하고 싶었고, 그렇게 Rust crate 하나를 오랜 기간에 걸쳐 드디어 만들어내게 되었습니다!

작년부터 공부해온 지식으로, 올해 초부터 코드를 한줄씩 쌓아올렸고, 이제는 무려 1만줄에 가까운 양의 리포가 되었습니다. 소소하지만 이번에 첫 버전을 이렇게 공개해봅니다.

item.title: Trying to get our Arms around AI efficiency
item.content:encoded: Ryan sits down with Alex Spinelli, Senior Vice President of AI and Developer Platforms at Arm, for a conversation about bringing ML capabilities to edge devices, adapting software tools to meet the unique demands of autonomous agents, and the critical importance of prioritizing functional safety as artificial intelligence transitions into the physical world of robotics.

item.title: Chaos, then control: the maturity model most AI rollouts skip over
item.content:encoded: Every engineering org has rolled out AI coding tools by now, but far fewer have actually seen the outcomes they were hoping for.

item.title: The pioneering coding tricks that built Doom and Quake
item.content:encoded: Ryan chats with John Romero, creator of the WAD file and the video game Doom, about the self-modifying code and blitting techniques that made Wolfenstein run so fast on early PCs, the mod-friendly architecture that turned Doom into a cultural phenomenon, and why the raw creative problem-solving of Quake proves that human ideas will always beat AI coding agents.

item.title: Your coding agent shouldn't grade its own homework
item.content:encoded: AI coding agents can now write design docs, mock up frontends, and implement entire projects end to end. But can they be trusted to verify that their own code actually works?

item.title: Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers
item.content:encoded: Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.

item.title: How do you hire a human? Q&A with Tom Harvey, Stack Overflow technical recruiter
item.content:encoded: Everybody's resume is perfect now, so how do you find the perfect teammate?

item.title: Customer support is the gnarliest AI problem
item.content:encoded: Ryan chats with Ahmad Al-Dahle, CTO at Airbnb, about deploying multi-party AI agents to tackle the uniquely gnarly problem of customer support, how a moving target of rigorous evaluations helps engineers balance latency against accuracy, and the ways in which AI coding tools demand an even higher level of judgment from software engineering teams.

item.title: Never Share Your Password Again — The OAuth 2.0 Solution
Welcome to life in the chip age
item.content:encoded: Ryan sits down with Rakesh Kumar, professor of computer engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, to talk about the astounding complexity of manufacturing modern semiconductors, the massive environmental and geopolitical footprint of AI data centers, and how AI models are rapidly shifting the future of chip design.

item.title: Don’t Build the Reusable Component Yet
Your .NET parallel loop can become serial in a one-CPU container
item.content:encoded: CPU-based defaults can leave an I/O-heavy loop processing one record at a time. Raising the limit helps, but each downstream service still needs a concurrency budget it can handle.

item.title: Oh, your agents need OAuth2, too
item.content:encoded: Recorded at LDX3 by LeadDev, Ryan chats with Dan Moore, Senior Director of CIAM Strategy and Identity Standards at FusionAuth, about adapting established OAuth2 protocols for the agentic era, the security necessity of giving autonomous AI agents their own distinct identities, and how AI coding tools are shifting developers' focus toward solving core business problems.

item.title: It’s ok that computers are (sometimes) better than us
item.content:encoded: Ryan is joined by Charity Majors, co-founder and CTO at Honeycomb, for a conversation about applying the concept of immutable infrastructure to software development to treat code like cattle instead of pets, shifting the paradigm of system specifications to accommodate the rapid influx of AI-generated code, and navigating the complex ethical boundaries between system observability and human surveillance in modern technology ecosystems.

item.title: The reports of Stack Overflow's death are greatly exaggerated
item.content:encoded: I’ve seen the recent predictions about Stack Overflow’s demise. They make for compelling headlines, but they confuse a change in how people access knowledge with the disappearance of the knowledge—and the company—behind it.

item.title: A JSON schema Is not an AI governance layer
item.content:encoded: The AI governance argument is happening one layer above the code that actually stops your agent.

item.title: Delivering controlled and concentrated context
item.content:encoded: Check out the new features and capabilities now available in Stack Internal and Stack Internal Community. Try Stack Internal for free by visiting stackinternal.com.

item.title: Elevators, toasters, and the birth of Java
item.content:encoded: Ryan sits down with James Gosling, creator of Java at Sun Microsystems, to talk about the early networking friction that drove the need for interconnectedness, the stringent reliability requirements of consumer electronics companies that inspired the Java virtual machine, and the evolution of garbage collectors that allow Java to handle large-scale concurrent memory management.

item.title: Rumors of the SaaS demise are greatly exaggerated
item.content:encoded: Recorded on the floor of LDX3, Ryan chats with Nivia Henry, an engineering leader most recently at Netflix, about the reality of the supposed SaaS apocalypse, the complex calculus of the modern build-versus-buy decision in the era of AI, and the critical importance of understanding system architectures to manage long-term infrastructure costs.

item.title: The Regression Tests Nobody Writes: Capturing How Software Actually Behaves
Is AI really reshaping the developer market?
item.content:encoded: The market for developer jobs is shrinking, and it's getting harder to hire the engineers you need.

item.title: Building Immersive Virtual Economies: An Introduction to KursarScript (KSPL)
Survey Says: You'll swap the model, but everything you build around it is staying put
item.content:encoded: Earlier this month, my team at Stacklok surveyed 520 technical leaders to understand whether they were concerned about being locked into frontier labs. The data says they’re already swapping models in and out, but the trap they’re concerned about is the layer on top of the model.

item.title: Don't forget about the UI for AI
item.content:encoded: Recorded at OpenAI Dev Day 2026, Ryan sits down with Andrew Ambrosino, member of the technical staff at OpenAI, for a conversation on OpenAI's strategy for merging ChatGPT and Codex into a unified experience, the advantages of localized computer access in their successful desktop application, and the technical hurdles of constructing ChatGPT Spaces to support real-time multi-agent collaboration.

item.title: Production-grade LLMs and agents: a field guide
item.content:encoded: A maturity model for taking agents from an impressive demo to a system people can depend on — with a self-assessment and the map to a deep-dive on each layer.

item.title: AI says you’re right, formal methods say you’re wrong
item.content:encoded: Ryan is joined by Gabriela Moreira, CEO at Quint, about why formal specification languages like TLA+ are essential for catching system design flaws before writing code, how Quint brings developer-friendly syntax and executability to formal methods, and the ways trace validation and model-based testing can verify AI-generated code against real-world production data.

item.title: MCP standardized tools. Now we need the infrastructure around them.
Why your platform team shouldn't build an AI context layer (even though they probably could)
item.content:encoded: Most engineering teams capable of building an internal AI knowledge system think they should. But six months later, it's a platform team's full-time job. Building an in-house AI context layer costs more money and energy than you think.

item.title: Your next job doesn’t have a title yet: Emerging role skills Q&A with Cory Hymel of Andela
item.content:encoded: While the whispers say that everyone is becoming a generalist, that's not where headcount is going.

item.title: Why Your Sandbox Never Quite Matches Production (And Why That's Fine)
item.content:encoded: Sandbox testing works best when you stop chasing production parity. Learn what environment drift actually costs and which parts are worth fixing.

item.title: Keep calm and call clone with Rust
item.content:encoded: Ryan sits down with Josh Triplett, member of the Rust Leadership Team at the Rust Project, to chat about how the borrow checker delivers compile-time memory safety without garbage collection overhead, why Rust consistently ranks as developers' most loved language by providing psychological safety for complex systems, and how strict compiler constraints make Rust an ideal target for AI coding agents.

item.title: Beyond the AI noise: How Stack Overflow is rethinking tech hiring
item.content:encoded: It’s gotten exponentially harder to identify talent that we feel is a good fit for our teams at the top of the application funnel.

item.title: A Treatise on Model Oriented Programming Languages
Taking a look under your agent’s hood
item.content:encoded: Ryan is joined by Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer at Datadog, to talk about applying observability to non-deterministic AI agents, blurring the boundaries between software development and production workflows, and navigating emerging challenges in AI security and tokenomics.

item.title: Part 5: Operating an LLM system: observability, cost, routing, and the platform underneath
item.content:encoded: Your service can be 100% up and still quietly approving the wrong things, burning its budget, or failing over into untested quality. Level 5 is the infrastructure that lets you see your decisions, bound your spend, route and fail over between models, kill bad behavior in seconds — and the platform that makes all of it possible.
